title: About
text:
I’m a third-year Geomatics student at the University of Waterloo, with a minor in Computing. Geomatics brings together most of what I enjoy: computer science, geography, maps and data science.
I like making things, whether that’s code, a map, or a 3D view of a LiDAR point cloud, and I enjoy finding the visualization that makes a dataset click. Sometimes that extends to hardware, like building a GPS logger or writing sensor drivers for a Nordic Thingy:53, so I can collect the data myself.
Next, I want professional experience in remote sensing, especially RPAS, LiDAR and radar, and I’d love to work with geospatial data in less familiar terrain like the Arctic. I’m looking for co-op opportunities where I can build those skills on real-world, meaningful projects. My next co-op terms are back-to-back running from January 2027 to April 2027, and then from May 2027 to August 2027.

title: Geocoding 24 years of Kitchener building permits
text: New construction permits, 1999–2022, aggregated to a 0.25 km² hexagon grid.

title: Geocoding 24 years of Kitchener building permits
text:
Approach
The permit records had street addresses but no coordinates. I built an address locator from the city’s address-point layer, geocoded every permit, cleaned the results, and filtered to the “new construction” type. To make the patterns readable, I aggregated permits to a hexagonal grid and enabled time on the layer to animate it year by year.



Matched
Unmatched
Tied
Match rate




69,830
2,729
1
96.2 %



I checked the unmatched addresses (for example, 2396 King St E) and found they point to locations in the middle of a road rather than a building. That’s why they’re missing from the city’s list of valid addresses: the problem is in the permit records, not the locator.

title: Geocoding 24 years of Kitchener building permits
text:
Results
New construction is concentrated on the edges of the city, in Trussler, Huron Park, Doon South, Williamsburg, Beechwood Forest and Grand River South. Those are the residential areas that grew during this period. A few cells near the core and along major roads pass 60 permits.

  




Permits issued per year.


Two peaks stand out: 2002–2007, during a period of strong residential growth, and 2014–2016, which lines up with ION light rail construction.

title: Geocoding 24 years of Kitchener building permits
text:
Limitations

Hexagon counts reflect how many addresses fall in each cell as well as how much building happened, so dense subdivisions score higher partly because they have more addresses. Normalising by address count would separate the two.
The link between the 2014–2016 peak and ION construction is a correlation I noticed, not something I tested.

title: Siting wind farms in Huron County
text: Suitability for wind turbines across Huron County with the baseline weights (5 = most suitable).

title: Siting wind farms in Huron County
text:
Approach
1. Build the factors. I clipped every layer to the county. For each constraint I created four buffer rings, starting from a minimum setback (for example, 550 m from buildings) and getting more suitable with distance. I then converted each to a raster on a shared 1–5 suitability scale. The Wind Atlas data had to be converted in QGIS before ArcGIS Pro could read it.
2. Weight and overlay. I combined the six factors in a weighted overlay:



Factor
Weight




Wind speed at 30 m
30 %


Distance from buildings
20 %


Distance from airports
15 %


Distance from urban areas
15 %


Distance from roads
10 %


Distance from wooded areas
10 %



Wind speed gets the most weight because without wind there’s no power. Buildings come next because they block wind and signal people nearby. Roads and woodland come last because they can be built around or cleared.
3. Test the weights. The weights are a judgement call, so I tested how much the answer depends on them. I reduced each factor’s weight in 10 % steps, from 90 % of its value down to 10 %, and redistributed the difference to the others. That gave 54 alternative suitability rasters. I then took the per-cell standard deviation across all 54 and classed cells with low variation (below 0.25) as stable.






Per-cell standard deviation across the 54 weight scenarios. Darker cells change less when the weights change.







Cells whose suitability stays stable under every weighting (green).

title: Siting wind farms in Huron County
text:
Result
A good site has to be both highly suitable with the baseline weights (class 4–5) and stable across the sensitivity runs. Large stable areas in the centre of the county were ruled out because they’re stable at only moderate or low suitability. Two areas pass both tests:






Site 1: northern and southern Ashfield-Colborne-Wawanosh.







Site 2: centre-west to north-west Bluewater, near the Lake Huron shore where wind speeds are highest.

title: Siting wind farms in Huron County
text:
Limitations

The 1–5 scores for each buffer ring are assumptions. A real study would base setbacks on Ontario’s renewable energy regulations and add constraints like protected areas and grid connection.
Wind Atlas data is a modelled long-term average at 30 m, below a modern turbine’s hub height.

title: Mapping police occurrences in Waterloo Region
text: Total 2023 occurrences in 0.5 km² hexagons, with an inset of the City of Waterloo.

title: Mapping police occurrences in Waterloo Region
text:
Approach
The occurrence CSV stored each location as one UTM “easting, northing” text field, which ArcGIS Pro can’t plot. I split it into separate coordinate columns, converted the records to points, and aggregated them to a 0.5 km² hexagon grid. I mapped total occurrences and individual types (assaults, fires and others) two ways: as a hexagon choropleth and as graduated symbols. Each map includes an inset of the City of Waterloo around the two universities and the college.

title: Mapping police occurrences in Waterloo Region
text:

Total occurrences as graduated symbols.

title: Mapping police occurrences in Waterloo Region
text:
Results
Occurrences concentrate in the cores of Kitchener, Waterloo and Cambridge, with cells reaching several times the counts of the surrounding townships. Around the post-secondary campuses, activity clusters along University Avenue between Wilfrid Laurier and the east side of the University of Waterloo, the busiest stretch between the institutions.

title: Mapping police occurrences in Waterloo Region
text:
Limitations

These are raw counts. Because the cities hold most of the population, counts largely track where people are. Dividing by population or by daytime activity would show where occurrences are disproportionately high.
Recorded occurrences depend on reporting, so lower counts in rural areas partly reflect fewer people around to report incidents.

title: Remote sensing toolkit: classification, radar and LiDAR
text: Three lab projects from my remote sensing course, each with a different sensor: a multispectral satellite, a radar satellite and airborne laser scanning.

title: Remote sensing toolkit: classification, radar and LiDAR
text:
1. Comparing land-cover classifiers, Hamilton–Burlington
I classified a Landsat 8 scene of Hamilton and Burlington into seven land-cover classes (water, forest, other vegetation, light and dark bare soil, residential, and commercial/industrial). I used five methods, trained on the same samples, and assessed each against 425 check points.



Method
Overall accuracy
Kappa




Object-based SVM
90.1 %
0.88


Random trees (per-pixel)
89.6 %
0.88


Support vector machine (per-pixel)
89.2 %
0.87


Maximum likelihood (per-pixel)
82.8 %
0.80


ISO Cluster (unsupervised)
Very low
n/a









The five classifiers compared over water and shoreline, beside a false-colour composite.







The same comparison over an urban area. Several classifiers confuse road edges with bare soil, and the object-based result is blocky.





Water was classified almost perfectly because its spectral signature is so distinct. The main confusion was between forest and other vegetation, and between light and dark soil. The most useful lesson was about assessment. The unsupervised result looked reasonable on the map but scored very poorly against the check points, and the object-based result scored best despite looking blocky. Points sample single pixels, so polygon-based or denser check samples would give a fairer accuracy measure.

title: Remote sensing toolkit: classification, radar and LiDAR
section: 2. Radar: forest change and InSAR elevation
text:
2. Radar: forest change and InSAR elevation
Forest change. I compared Sentinel-1 scenes from February 2017 and February 2018 over forest in Roraima, Brazil, using a speckle-filtered RGB composite (R = VH, G = VV, B = VH/VV). VH responds to canopy volume and VV to bare surfaces, so the composite shows canopy as green and gaps as brown. This made the change in cover between the two years easy to see.






2017 composite (R = VH, G = VV, B = VH/VV).







2018 composite with the same band assignment, showing more continuous canopy.





Elevation from interferometry. From a Sentinel-1 pair six days apart (perpendicular baseline 174 m), I generated an interferogram, unwrapped the phase, converted it to elevation, and compared the result with the SRTM DEM. Areas of high coherence gave clean fringes, and the InSAR DEM reproduced the main terrain seen in SRTM. Low-coherence areas produced noise, and the unwrapping showed faint tile seams.






Wrapped interferogram (top) and unwrapped phase (bottom).







Coherence (top), SRTM DEM (middle) and the Sentinel-1 InSAR DEM (bottom).

title: Remote sensing toolkit: classification, radar and LiDAR
section: 3. LiDAR: classifying a point cloud, Laurel Creek, Waterloo
text:
3. LiDAR: classifying a point cloud, Laurel Creek, Waterloo
With LAStools, I classified a 1.2-million-return airborne LiDAR tile into ground, high vegetation and buildings. I then built a bare-earth DEM, a surface model and height-above-ground rasters at 0.5 m, using the Laurel Creek outline as a breakline.






Classified point cloud: ground (brown), high vegetation (green), buildings (orange), unclassified (grey).







The same cloud in 3D.

Height above ground for trees and buildings, with the six features I checked against field measurements.


I compared heights from the LiDAR rasters with field-measured heights for three trees and three buildings. Four of the six agreed to within about 1.6 m. One tree was off by 2–3 m and one building by over 4 m, which shows how much a single point measurement depends on where on the feature it’s taken. Water returned no points because the scanner’s near-infrared pulse is absorbed by water.

title: Sensor drivers to orientation on a Nordic Thingy:53
text:
Question


Can I bring up a board’s sensors from their datasheets, and fuse them into a usable orientation estimate?


Tools


C, Zephyr RTOS / nRF Connect SDK v2.5.1, devicetree overlays, Kconfig, I2C and SPI, Zephyr sensor API, SEGGER RTT


Hardware


Nordic Thingy:53 (nRF5340 with Bosch BME688, BMM150 and BMI270), nRF5340 DK as programmer and debugger


Context


Personal project, after completing Nordic Developer Academy’s nRF Connect SDK and Bluetooth LE Fundamentals courses
View the code on GitHub

title: Sensor drivers to orientation on a Nordic Thingy:53
section: Five apps, each building on the last
text:
Five apps, each building on the last








#
Sensor
What it does




01
BME688
Raw I2C temperature read with factory-calibration compensation (first attempt, started from a course exercise)


02
BME688
Temperature, pressure and humidity with the full calibration set


03
BMM150
3-axis magnetic field in µT from the chip’s trim registers

title: Sensor drivers to orientation on a Nordic Thingy:53
text:
What was involved

Register-level drivers. I read the data and calibration registers straight from the Bosch datasheets, reassembled multi-byte and bit-packed values, and handled signed calibration constants and the sign extension of 13- and 15-bit readings.
Order matters. On the BME688, humidity oversampling has to be written before the measurement-control register, because writing that register in forced mode starts a conversion immediately and a later humidity setting is ignored.
Compensation. The manufacturers’ formulas (the BME688 temperature, pressure and humidity polynomials, and the BMM150’s trim-based X/Y/Z compensation) turn raw ADC counts into physical units. A total field of about 60 µT was a good sanity check against Earth’s field.
Sensor fusion. Roll and pitch come from the gravity vector. Heading comes from projecting the magnetic field onto the horizontal plane using roll and pitch, so tilting the board doesn’t change the reported heading.

title: Sensor drivers to orientation on a Nordic Thingy:53
text:
Results

Sensor readings (apps 01–04)
Each driver was checked against what the physical quantity should be. Readings are from the RTT console with the board sitting still on a desk indoors.








App
Reading
Sanity check




01
22.96 °C
Plausible room temperature, steady to within 0.02 °C between samples


02
23.06 °C, 100.42 kPa, 51.9 % RH
Pressure within the normal range for air near the ground; humidity typical indoors


03
X −19.8, Y 11.4, Z −57.0 µT; total 61.4 µT
Inside Earth’s field range of about 25–65 µT. Z dominates, as expected at this latitude, where the field points steeply downward


04
Accel Z −9.86 m/s²; gyro below 0.01 rad/s
Gravity is 9.81 m/s². The gyro reads near zero at rest; the small offset is bias



App 01 had calibration bugs: one constant was read from the wrong buffer, and two signed constants were treated as unsigned. I left them as written in 01 and fixed them in 02, so the repo shows the progression.


Orientation and heading (app 05)
With the board held still, the orientation output behaves as expected: roll reads about ±1.59 rad (±91°) lying on either side, and pitch about ±1.5 rad standing on either end. Turning the board flat through the four compass directions gave these yaw changes:



Turn (flat, clockwise)
Yaw change




N → E
−1.70 rad


E → S
−1.66 rad


S → W
−1.38 rad


W → N
−1.55 rad



Each quarter-turn should be 1.57 rad, and the four steps add up to a full circle, so yaw tracks rotation correctly. It isn’t a compass heading yet, though: it decreases when turning clockwise, and it is measured from the board’s X axis rather than from north.

title: Sensor drivers to orientation on a Nordic Thingy:53
text:
Limitations and next steps

Calibration. The uneven quarter-turns (1.38–1.70 rad) come from missing hard- and soft-iron calibration; nearby metal and the board’s own electronics bias the field.
True north. Heading is magnetic. Correcting it means adding the local declination, about −10° in southern Ontario.
Motion. Accelerometer-only tilt breaks down while the board is moving. The gyroscope is read but not fused yet; a complementary or Madgwick filter is the next step.
AI use: AI was mainly used for debugging: finding register, calibration and sign-handling errors in the drivers. It occasionally helped me interpret register descriptions. The register maps and compensation formulas come from the Bosch datasheets, and the sensor bring-up and the progression to sensor fusion were my own work.

title: GPS and temperature field logger
text:
The logged drive between Burlington and Hamilton, about 7,300 fixes at 1 Hz, coloured by GPS elevation. Basemap tiles © Esri and contributors.
View the code on GitHub

title: GPS and temperature field logger
text:
Why I built it
I wanted to practise the full path from sensor to deliverable: wiring the hardware, writing the firmware, collecting data in the field, then parsing, fusing and transforming it into something useful. The test was a two-hour round-trip drive between Burlington and Hamilton, Ontario.



The logger: an Arduino Uno with the GPS and SD logging shield, external antenna and TMP36 sensor.

title: GPS and temperature field logger
text:
How it works
Firmware. The sketch reads NMEA sentences from the GPS on a timer interrupt and writes the RMC and GGA sentences to the SD card once per second. Every 10 seconds, when the GPS has a fix, it reads the TMP36 and writes a timestamped line to a separate log. It is based on Adafruit’s shield_sdlog example; I added the temperature sensor, the second log file and the fix-gated logging.
Processing. A Python script (also available as a notebook):

Parses the raw $GPGGA sentences for UTC time, satellite count, position (converted from degrees and decimal minutes) and altitude, and $GPRMC for speed over ground.
Fuses the 0.1 Hz temperature stream with the 1 Hz position stream by joining on time and linearly interpolating temperature to 1 Hz.
Transforms WGS84 geodetic coordinates to Earth-Centred Earth-Fixed (X, Y, Z), then rotates them into a local East-North-Up frame with its origin at the first fix.
Plots the drive in all three frames.

title: GPS and temperature field logger
text:
Results






ECEF: the global Cartesian frame, in metres from Earth’s centre. Correct, but hard to read at site scale.







ENU: metres east, north and up from the first fix, which reads directly at site scale.





The ENU view is the practical one for local work: every position reads as metres east, north and up from a chosen origin, which is how a survey or a robot would use it. ECEF is the necessary intermediate step. The climb onto the Niagara Escarpment on the Hamilton side shows clearly in the vertical axis.

title: GPS and temperature field logger
text:
Notes and limitations

Privacy: the published logs are trimmed to remove everything within 1.5 km of the start and end points.
Elevation comes from single-frequency GPS, so it is noisy, as the spikes in the ENU plot show.
Temperature was logged to practise merging datasets with different sampling rates, and isn’t plotted because it varied little over the drive.
AI use: the parsing and plotting code was written with AI assistance. My focus was the hardware build, field data collection and the geodetic → ECEF → ENU workflow.

title: GIS on a basketball court: shot accuracy maps
text: Kyle Lowry’s shooting percentage by court location, 2017–18 season.

title: GIS on a basketball court: shot accuracy maps
text:
Approach
Shot locations come in court coordinates, not latitude and longitude. I used a court image as the reference frame, plotted every shot as a point on it, and aggregated the shots into a hexagon grid. For each cell I calculated made ÷ attempted and classed it from 0–10 % up to over 75 %. The same workflow handles filtered subsets, such as one player or the team without that player.

title: GIS on a basketball court: shot accuracy maps
text:
Results






The 2017–18 Raptors as a team.







The Raptors without Lowry: almost identical to the full team.





Lowry was most accurate around the left, top and top-right of the three-point line, while the team as a whole was strongest just inside the arc. Removing Lowry barely changes the team map because his shots are a small share of the total.

title: GIS on a basketball court: shot accuracy maps
section: Comparing LeBron James vs Michael Jordan’s last game
text:
Comparing LeBron James vs Michael Jordan’s last game






LeBron James, 2022–23.







Michael Jordan, 2002–03 (his final season).





Both are highly accurate at the rim and in pockets of the mid-range. Jordan took far more mid-range shots, while James took more shots at or just behind the three-point line.

title: GIS on a basketball court: shot accuracy maps
text:
Limitations

Cells with only a handful of attempts can show 0 % or 100 % by chance. A minimum-attempts threshold, or shading by attempt count, would make the maps more honest.

title: Kitbash Builder: a parts library for 3D-printed miniatures
text:
The Parts Builder: twelve part slots on the left, and the bundle being assembled on the right.
View the code on GitHub

title: Kitbash Builder: a parts library for 3D-printed miniatures
text:
What it does

Indexes once. A single pass reads every STL, measures it, and renders a thumbnail and a lightweight preview mesh into a SQLite database. Reclassifying after that takes seconds and never re-reads the files.
Classifies by name and size. Keyword rules on file and folder names decide each part’s slot (head, torso, arm, weapon…), its faction and its armour pattern. Measured size checks the guesses: a 12 mm file can’t be a 32 mm figure, whatever it is called.
Corrects scale. Sculptors export in very different units, so each pack gets a scale factor from its confidently identified parts, and parts are rescaled to match the torso you build around.
Handles messy downloads. It recognises supported copies, pre-sliced printer plates, revision folders and images saved with a .stl extension, and exports one raw copy of each part.
Learns from corrections. A review workflow writes a spreadsheet per folder; verdicts imported back override the rules on every later run.
Extracts archives safely. A companion script unpacks nested downloads without running anything, blocking path traversal, links, executable bits and archive bombs.

title: Kitbash Builder: a parts library for 3D-printed miniatures
text:
About the project
I planned and designed this tool for my own hobby of 3D printing and painting miniatures. AI (Claude) wrote all of the code and the documentation. No model files are included in the repository; it is meant for organising a collection you already own.

title: Tracking wildfire forest loss with Sentinel-1 radar
text: 2023 forest cover (green) and forest lost since the previous year (red) across the study area, from Sentinel-1 VH/VV backscatter.

title: Tracking wildfire forest loss with Sentinel-1 radar
text:
Why radar
The 2023 fire season burned large parts of northern Quebec. Optical imagery struggles with exactly what wildfires produce: smoke and cloud. Sentinel-1 is an active C-band radar, so it sees through both, day or night. I chose the VH (cross-polarised) band because it responds to volume scattering in tree canopies, and VV because it picks up surface scattering where the canopy is gone. At the AI assistant’s suggestion, I also added the VH/VV ratio to separate canopy from wetlands, which are common in the region and otherwise look like forest.



Study area: roughly 49.5–54.5° N, 74–80° W, from the James Bay coast inland.

title: Tracking wildfire forest loss with Sentinel-1 radar
text:
Approach

Composites. For each year, I built a median composite of all Sentinel-1 scenes from June to September (widened to May–October when coverage was thin), using both orbit directions to avoid gaps.
Forest threshold. I set the forest threshold from the data itself: the 55th percentile of 2020 VH backscatter. A pixel counts as forest if it is above that threshold and its VH/VV ratio is above −8 dB.
Burn detection. Comparing each year with the one before, I flagged a pixel as burned if its VH backscatter dropped by more than 2 dB.
Area. I summed the forest and burned pixels using their true geodetic area, at 500 m resolution to stay within Earth Engine’s computation limits, and converted to km² for each year.

title: Tracking wildfire forest loss with Sentinel-1 radar
text:
Results



Forest cover (green, left axis) and newly burned forest (red, right axis) per year. The two axes have very different scales.


The burned-area signal peaks at about 2,400 km² in 2024, with a smaller rise in 2023. Forest cover ranges between about 70,000 and 110,000 km².

title: Tracking wildfire forest loss with Sentinel-1 radar
text:
Evaluating the result
The brief asked me to judge the AI-assisted workflow, and the numbers themselves show where it falls short:

Forest cover swings more than the landscape can. Forest area rises by 10,000–15,000 km² in single years (2021 and 2025), which is far faster than planting or regrowth could produce a canopy radar would see. The drop from 2021 to 2024 (about 41,000 km²) is also much larger than the burned area detected (about 3,700 km²). Some of that could be harvesting, which this method doesn’t separate from fire, but a threshold set from 2020 data, year-to-year differences in moisture and scene coverage, and gaps in some years’ coverage likely account for much of it.
Timing. The largest burn signal appears a year after the 2023 fires. Because each year is compared with the previous summer’s composite, fires that happened during or after a summer’s imaging window likely only show up in the next year’s comparison.
Coarse area estimates. Summing at 500 m keeps the computation within Earth Engine’s limits but blurs small burns and forest edges.
No validation. Checking the burned pixels against the national fire perimeter database would turn these results from plausible into measured.

AI use: I used ChatGPT first, and then Claude when ChatGPT’s scripts kept failing. I set the problem, the data choice and the requirements, worked through the empty-layer and memory-limit problems with follow-up prompts, and evaluated the output. The assistant wrote the Earth Engine code.

title: Where should the next fire station go?
text: Travel time of 10 minutes or less from the current stations plus both proposed sites, with recorded fire calls.

title: Where should the next fire station go?
text:
The question
In this scenario, the region is weighing two sites for a new fire station: New Hamburg in the west and Elmira in the north. I compared how each one would change response times and workload across the existing 16-station network.

title: Where should the next fire station go?
text:
Approach

Travel-time cost. I added a travel-time field to every road segment (length ÷ posted speed, in minutes) and built a network dataset with that cost and a one-way restriction.
Service areas. I generated 2-, 5- and 10-minute drive-time polygons for the current network, each proposed site on its own, and every combination.
Location-allocation. I assigned every recorded fire call to its nearest station by drive time under four scenarios (current, + New Hamburg, + Elmira, + both), then summarised average response time, calls left outside the 10-minute area, and calls per station.

title: Where should the next fire station go?
text:
Results









Scenario
Avg. response time
Calls outside 10 min
Calls allocated to new station




Current stations
3.06 min

+ Elmira
2.89 min

On average response time and coverage the two sites are nearly tied. Each cuts the average by about 10 seconds and brings roughly 130 more calls inside the 10-minute area. The difference shows up on the map. Most calls near Elmira are already reached within 10 minutes by the existing network, and the region north of Elmira has very few calls. New Hamburg covers a cluster of calls on the western edge that the current network barely reaches, and it takes on 27 more calls than Elmira would.






New Hamburg on its own: the 10-minute area covers the western cluster of calls.







Elmira on its own: much of its area overlaps calls the existing network already reaches.





Recommendation: build at New Hamburg. It relieves more of the network, serves an area the current stations don’t reach quickly, and matches Elmira on average response time.



The current 16-station network for comparison.

title: Where should the next fire station go?
text:
Limitations

Travel times use posted speed limits with no turn penalties, traffic or emergency-vehicle behaviour, so absolute times are optimistic. The comparison between sites is more reliable than the minutes themselves.
The analysis uses one historical set of calls. A full siting study would also look at population growth and where calls are likely to come from in future.
